name: midicsv
desc: Convert MIDI audio files to human-readable CSV format
why: Turning MIDI binaries into readable CSV is a clear way to see how a music file is structured.

brief.what_it_is: midicsv is a pair of command-line programs by John Walker (Fourmilab). midicsv reads a standard MIDI file and writes a CSV text file that records every event in it, one event per line, with track number, absolute time, and event type as the first fields. csvmidi reads a CSV file in that same format and writes an equivalent MIDI file. Both read standard input and write standard output, so they can sit in a Unix pipeline between text tools.
brief.why_it_exists: The author's framing is that MIDI files are compact binary files that are hard to read and write without a special-purpose library, while Perl and Python are well suited to the transformations musicians want. The programs are meant to let text-processing tools transform MIDI files, or generate them from scratch, in bulk.
brief.how_it_works: midicsv decodes the binary MIDI file into records such as 'Track, Time, Note_on_c, Channel, Note, Velocity', with each event type given a readable name and a '_c' suffix for channel events or '_t' suffix for text meta-events. Records are sorted by track, then time, and the file opens with a Header record and closes with End_of_file. csvmidi parses those records back into binary MIDI and reports errors as warnings on standard error, skipping bad records. The README includes Perl examples (transpose, chorus, channel extraction, a drum machine, and a random guitar composer) that edit or generate the CSV.

commands_seen.context: Pipeline from the Transpose Key example: converts song.mid to CSV, shifts note numbers down an octave with a Perl filter (skipping channel 9 percussion), then rebuilds a MIDI file as tsong.mid.
Pipeline from the Chorus example: duplicates each non-percussion note one octave lower to thicken the bass, then writes the result as MIDI.
Pipeline from the Extract Channel example: keeps only events on the chosen channel (set to 9 for the General MIDI percussion track) and writes the result as MIDI.
Dumbest Drummer example: the Perl script prints CSV for a simple repeating drum pattern with no source MIDI file, and csvmidi turns it into drumtrack.mid.
Stoned Guitarist example: the Perl script writes CSV for a randomly generated guitar line with cymbal accompaniment and a closing applause effect, and csvmidi writes performance.mid.

brief.install_notes: The archive midicsv-1.1.tar.gz contains source, a Makefile for Unix systems, and ready-to-run 32-bit Windows executables; a zipped archive with only the Windows executables is also offered. Building from source uses the supplied Makefile. The Perl examples need Perl, and the README suggests TiMidity++ as a software synthesiser for listening to the results. I did not see Homebrew-specific steps; the executables listed are csvmidi and midicsv.
brief.standout: The CSV format is designed on purpose to be easy for text tools, spreadsheets, and databases to handle, and the author states that no information is lost on a round trip. Its examples show that a short script can edit or generate a whole MIDI file through a pipe, which is a different approach from a sequencer or a MIDI library.
brief.status: quiet. The README is dated 'by John Walker, February, 2004, Revised January, 2008', and the latest download it names is midicsv-1.1.tar.gz. The page gives no newer release or commit history, so the project looks finished rather than actively developed. I did not check a repository or the Homebrew formula for more recent versions.
brief.caveats: midicsv assumes its input is a well-formed MIDI file. Gross errors may crash it, and it does not check for things like a note-on without a matching note-off. csvmidi does not do semantic checking either, so a CSV that is well-formed but musically nonsensical will produce a MIDI file that instruments may not play sensibly. The round trip is equivalent but not guaranteed to be byte-for-byte identical, because the -x option controls MIDI running-status compression. The Windows executables are 32-bit. The software is public domain with no warranty. The homepage was reachable and the README is the homepage itself.
quotes: No information is lost in transforming a MIDI file to CSV and back.
MIDI files are somewhat difficult to read and write without a special-purpose library, particularly in commonly used text processing languages such as Perl and Python
This program isn't presented for its musical merit, but simply to illustrate how easy it is to generate arbitrary MIDI music files by writing CSV which is fed through csvmidi.
